editor_spans.body: The speech explains the decline of Motherwell and Leigh in a particular way. Ravenscraig and the Lancashire pits were lost to decisions 'taken hundreds of miles away' by people who never lived with what followed, and nobody in Whitehall came to talk about what would happen next. But the powers on offer do not touch decisions like those. Devolved employment support, regional innovation money and better training routes all prepare people for jobs that someone else decides to create or close. Ravenscraig did not shut because Lanarkshire lacked a jobcentre that knew people by name.

The present-day versions of Ravenscraig are mentioned in the speech, but only briefly. On Grangemouth the government is 'working with' Holyrood to 'help secure' new investment. On Aberdeen, which is living through the same loss of good jobs, there will be 'more to say in due course'. The UK government keeps the decisions that will settle what happens to the North Sea and the refinery site. Regions and Holyrood are offered the job of dealing with the consequences. Under the Prime Minister's own account, that is how the 1990s went wrong. The test is whether, when Aberdeen's turn comes, anyone there gets a say over what happens to the industry, not just over the employment schemes that follow.

The 'Easterhouse principle' has a contradiction built into it. The speech says the project worked because it was 'run by the local community and the people on the estate'. Yet the plan is to make it 'the way we support everybody, everywhere' across a whole nation, using money from the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP). An approach designed for a single estate, once rolled out by a state body, risks turning into exactly the centrally designed scheme the speech rejects. The evidence offered is also anecdotal: one visit, and a Greater Manchester Live Well model said to have achieved 'more than we could have imagined', with no numbers given. That is a weak basis for a nationwide change to employment support.

This builds on my earlier point that the offer to Holyrood is a way to compete with it on its own ground. The full speech shows how. Scotland, it says, is 'one of the most centralised nations in Europe'. The Scottish Government's own local government reform is too slow. A proposal designed in Westminster is presented as a question to the First Minister: 'Do you?'. If Holyrood says yes, the Prime Minister gets credit for powering up Scottish regions. If it hesitates, it looks like the centre that will not let go. Either way, the argument about where power should sit in Scotland moves away from Holyrood versus Westminster and towards Holyrood versus its own cities. That is likely to outlast whatever the National Economic Council agrees.

Story 5, from "Prime Minister makes offer to Holyrood to work together to empower Scottish regions", published 2026-10-15, from govuk-number-10; cited by 1 later Editor's Span
  · Because power was never supposed to stop at the doors of the Scottish Parliament, the Prime Minister will argue the next stage of devolution should place more decision-making in the hands of Scotland’s regions and cities to drive reindustrialisation.
  S352 (mentioning Andy Burnham {Q269909}, Scottish Government {Q32521}, Government of the United Kingdom {Q6063}, Number 10 North {Q140382294}, Scotland Office {Q277020}, Scotland {Q22}): As part of that offer, ⟦Andy Burnham⟧ will call on the Scottish Government to work with the UK Government through No10 North and the Scotland Office to develop a new model of regional empowerment for Scotland, ensuring communities with their own strengths, identity and ambitions can seize new economic opportunities and unlock their potential.
  · During my first week in office, I told the First Minister that I wanted to work with ⟦Scotland’s First Minister⟧ to spread opportunities to communities across Scotland’s regions and cities.
  S353 (spoken by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, mentioning Number 10 North {Q140382294}): Through No10 North, we are rewiring the state and I want to make sure regions in Scotland are fully part of this.
  · This is me making an offer to the Scottish Government.

Story 435, the Editor's, made 2026-10-24: "Read together, three announcements from one week show a single political strategy: Great British Railways' headquarters going to Derby, the 'No10 North' offer to Holyrood, and the apprenticeship pledges. Each moves institutions and decisions away from London. The Scotland offer goes further. It turns Westminster's devolution argument against the Scottish Government, calling it 'one of the most centralised devolved administrations in Europe.' That gives the Prime Minister a way to compete with Holyrood on its own ground while appearing to offer cooperation."; cited by no later Editor's Span
  S354 (the Editor's): Read together, three announcements from one week show a single political strategy: Great British Railways' headquarters going to Derby, the 'No10 North' offer to Holyrood, and the apprenticeship pledges. Each moves institutions and decisions away from London. The Scotland offer goes further. It turns Westminster's devolution argument against the Scottish Government, calling it 'one of the most centralised devolved administrations in Europe.' That gives the Prime Minister a way to compete with Holyrood on its own ground while appearing to offer cooperation.
  · The timing for the railway is worth noting. Building at Becketwell starts in early 2027 and is due to finish by spring 2029. That is close to the latest date for the next general election, so the building meant to embody public ownership may only just be ready before voters judge it. Until then, the claimed benefits depend on things a minister can announce, such as a fare freeze and extra seats, rather than an organisation that already exists. The headline 600 apprenticeships are also spread over four years and sit within a much bigger youth employment scheme.
